Work  /  Cambridge Montessori School
Identity · Information design · Publications · Campaign

A century-old pedagogy, made legible in three colors.

Montessori is easy to admire and hard to explain. The system had to make a 1911 developmental theory something a parent could understand on a school tour — and hold in one hand.

Client

Cambridge Montessori School

Services

Identity, information design, publications, advertising

Scope

Logo, signage, curriculum map, guides, transit, strategic plan

Sub-brand

Passport Summer · Extended Day · Clubs

Exterior signage. Toddler through Middle School, stated plainly at the door.

The challenge

In 1911 Maria Montessori proposed that human development runs in four roughly six-year Planes of Development. It is the foundation of the whole method — and to a parent touring a school with a three-year-old in tow, it is an abstraction delivered by someone using words like “absorbent mind.”

Independent schools live or die on enrollment, and enrollment turns on a parent understanding what makes this school different from the one down the road. The pedagogy is the differentiator. If it can’t be explained, it can’t be sold.

Harder still: the school spans 21 months to Grade 8. One family may be choosing a toddler program while another weighs a middle school. Same institution, radically different questions.

The idea

Give each plane a color, then carry it absolutely everywhere. Orange, green and red — on the brochure, the curriculum map, the program icons, the signage, and, quietly, in the three dots of the logo itself.

The mark is three figures holding a circle between them, with three colored dots above. Those dots are the planes. A parent will never be told that, and does not need to be — by the time they reach the curriculum map, the colors are already familiar.

Plane 01

Absorbent Mind

21 months – Kindergarten

Toddler, Primary and Kindergarten. Learning through the senses, movement and repetition.

Plane 02

Cosmic Expansion

Grades 1–6

Lower and Upper Elementary. Concrete to abstract; the imagination set loose on history and the universe.

Plane 03

Cultural Integration

Grades 7–8

Middle School. Identity, social self, and academic work with real consequences.

The accordion brochure: one panel per plane, color-coded, in sequence.
The curriculum guide. The philosophy gets a spread before any subject does.

The centerpiece

The curriculum map is the piece that does the persuading: three planes down, seven subject areas across — language and literacy, mathematics, science, technology, cultural studies, Spanish and the arts, social curriculum and PE.

Every cell answers the same question at a different age. A parent can read one row to understand a stage, or one column to follow a subject from 21 months to Grade 8. The entire academic program, on one sheet, folding down to something that fits in a bag.

That is the argument a tour cannot make. It is also the piece a parent still has on the kitchen table three weeks later.

Three planes down, seven subjects across. The whole program in one view.

Out in the city

Two words, an imperative, and a child doing something absorbing. Discover Learning. Nurture Curiosity. No mention of pedagogy — that argument is for the map, once someone is already interested. Transit gets the feeling; the print gets the reasoning.

Platform billboard.
Concourse panel.

The same system, doing other jobs

The strategic plan takes the identical logic to a different audience — five pillars, five colors, one poster each. Board and community material built out of the same kit as the admissions material, which is how a small school stops looking like five different organizations.

Program · Faculty & Staff · CMS Community · Financial · Facilities.

Passport

The summer day camp had to sell to families who had never heard of the school — so it got its own warmer, louder identity, tied back only by the school’s mark sitting inside the O. Fourteenth year of operation, ages 21 months to 13 years, campers from all over.

The parent system’s logic carries through. Named, color-banded age tiers — Explorers, Discoverers, Navigators — do exactly what the three planes do on the school side: give a parent one obvious place to look for their own child. The difference is register. The school explains a pedagogy; the camp sounds like travel.

The full suite: cover, welcome spread, program spreads and back cover with the AMS accreditation seal.

The outcome

Passport camp enrollment has since tripled. The camp was the part of the system with the clearest before and after — a standalone identity, its own brochure, its own age tiers, sold to families with no prior connection to the school.

The school never published formal figures, and design was never the only variable — programming expanded and word of mouth compounds. But a camp that has to win families who have never heard of you is the closest thing to a controlled test a school offers, and it tripled.
